payload.statement_nl: Let h be a nonnegative integer. A numerical semigroup is a cofinite additive submonoid of the nonnegative integers containing 0, and its genus is the number of nonnegative integers not belonging to it. For a numerical semigroup Lambda, let F(Lambda) be the largest integer not in Lambda, with the convention F(Lambda) = -1 for the whole set of nonnegative integers. A minimal generator of Lambda is a positive element x of Lambda that cannot be written as a+b with positive a,b in Lambda. An effective generator of Lambda is a minimal generator x satisfying x > F(Lambda). Let e(Lambda) be the number of effective generators of Lambda. Let N(k) be the number of numerical semigroups of genus k. For each integer r >= 0, let n_h(r) be the number of genus-h numerical semigroups Lambda with e(Lambda) = r. Then N(h+1) is equal to the sum, over all genus-h numerical semigroups Lambda, of e(Lambda). Equivalently, N(h+1) is equal to the sum, over all integers r >= 0, of r * n_h(r). All displayed sums are finite.

result_payload.proof_nl:
Fix h ≥ 0. Let
A = { (Λ, x) : Λ is a numerical semigroup of genus h and x is an effective generator of Λ }
and
B = { S : S is a numerical semigroup of genus h+1 }.
By definition, N(h+1) = |B|.

We will prove that the map sending (Λ, x) to the set obtained from Λ by removing x is a bijection A → B.

First, take (Λ, x) ∈ A, and let S be Λ with x removed. Because x is a minimal generator, x is positive, so 0 still belongs to S. Since Λ is cofinite, removing one element keeps it cofinite. It remains to check closure under addition. Let a, b ∈ S. Since Λ is an additive submonoid, a+b ∈ Λ. If a+b were not in S, then necessarily a+b = x, because x is the only element removed from Λ. But x is not in S, so neither a nor b can be 0; hence a and b are positive. This contradicts the definition of x as a minimal generator of Λ, since x would then be written as a+b with positive a, b ∈ Λ. Therefore a+b ∈ S. So S is a numerical semigroup.

Its complement in the nonnegative integers is exactly the complement of Λ together with x. Hence the genus of S is h+1. Also, every integer not in Λ is at most F(Λ), and x > F(Λ) because x is effective. Therefore every integer greater than x belongs to Λ, and it still belongs to S because only x was removed. Since x itself is not in S, it follows that F(S) = x.

Thus the map φ : A → B defined by φ(Λ, x) = Λ with x removed is well-defined.

Conversely, take S ∈ B. Since h+1 > 0, S is not the whole set of nonnegative integers, so x := F(S) is an actual nonnegative integer not in S. Because 0 belongs to S, we have x > 0. Now let Λ := S ∪ {x}. Clearly 0 ∈ Λ, and adding one element to a cofinite set keeps it cofinite. We check closure under addition.

Let a, b ∈ Λ.
- If a and b both belong to S, then a+b ∈ S because S is a numerical semigroup.
- If one of a, b is x and the other is 0, then a+b = x ∈ Λ.
- In every other case, at least one summand is x and the other is positive, or both summands are x. Then a+b > x = F(S), so a+b belongs to S.

So Λ is a numerical semigroup. Its complement in the nonnegative integers is the complement of S with x removed, hence genus(Λ) = h.

We now show that x is an effective generator of Λ. First, x is minimal. Suppose, toward a contradiction, that x = a+b with positive a, b ∈ Λ. Then a < x and b < x. Since x is the only element added to S, this implies a, b ∈ S. But then closure of S gives x = a+b ∈ S, contradicting the definition of x = F(S). So x is a minimal generator of Λ.

Second, every integer not in Λ is also not in S and is different from x, so it is strictly less than x. Therefore F(Λ) < x. Hence x > F(Λ), so x is effective.

Thus the map ψ : B → A defined by ψ(S) = (S ∪ {F(S)}, F(S)) is well-defined.

The two maps are inverse. If (Λ, x) ∈ A, then from the first part we proved F(φ(Λ, x)) = x, so applying ψ to φ(Λ, x) adds back exactly x and recovers (Λ, x). If S ∈ B, then applying ψ adds F(S) and applying φ removes that same element, so one recovers S. Therefore φ is a bijection A ↔ B.

Now count A. For each fixed genus-h numerical semigroup Λ, the elements of A having first coordinate Λ are exactly the pairs (Λ, x) where x is an effective generator of Λ. There are exactly e(Λ) such pairs. Therefore, using the finiteness of the displayed sum,
|A| = sum over all genus-h numerical semigroups Λ of e(Λ).
Because A and B are bijective and N(h+1) = |B|, we obtain
N(h+1) = sum over all genus-h numerical semigroups Λ of e(Λ).

This proves the first displayed identity.

For the equivalent form, partition the genus-h numerical semigroups according to the value of e(Λ). For each integer r ≥ 0, let
C_r = { Λ : genus(Λ)=h and e(Λ)=r }.
By definition, |C_r| = n_h(r). The sets C_r partition the genus-h numerical semigroups, so, again using finiteness of the displayed sums,
sum over genus-h Λ of e(Λ)
= sum over r ≥ 0 of sum over Λ in C_r of e(Λ)
= sum over r ≥ 0 of sum over Λ in C_r of r
= sum over r ≥ 0 of r · n_h(r).
Combining this with the first identity gives
N(h+1) = sum from r=0 to infinity of r · n_h(r).

So both asserted identities hold, and the lemma is proved.
result_payload.proof_summary: Construct a bijection between genus-(h+1) numerical semigroups and pairs (Λ, x) where genus(Λ)=h and x is an effective generator of Λ: remove x from Λ, and inversely add the Frobenius number F(S) to a genus-(h+1) semigroup S. Counting these pairs gives N(h+1) = Σ e(Λ), and regrouping by the value r=e(Λ) gives N(h+1) = Σ r n_h(r).
